items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I knew guys, there were guys that played with Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, all these guys, that ended up in LA particularly, playing on movie dates.

ctx.x: You know there’s a great engineer/producer out in LA named Al Schmidt who is in his late 80s now. And I think he won a Grammy two years ago. He started out when he was a kid in New York. He’s one of the masters of all time. And he recorded in the early 60s Sam Cooke and people like that, up through Norah Jones. He’s still winning Grammys. He’s won I think 20, 22 Grammys. And Al told me one time, when I had one of those big dates, a roomful of players, one of the words of wisdom, “Just don’t let them see you…

when there was 35 people sitting out there and the tape machine would break right before the session, and we’d have to sit there for an hour. You’re looking at your watch and they’re looking at their watches. Because they know they’re only there for three hours; maybe two sessions, six hours. And you’ve got to get it. And the tape machine broke one time and we wasted an hour while they fixed that. The studio is not going to pay for those musicians. But we had to cram into two hours what we would have done in…
Yeah. I had a funny, Manny Albam had a funny anecdote about, I think he was producing the Guess Who.

items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: I mean Severinsen played with Tommy Dorsey, those guys were all, mostly big band alumni.

ctx.x: Well certainly, I wish I’d of lived in those times. Really, I mean I got to see the last of the big bands when I first started doing orchestra dates in L.A. String dates, orchestra dates, 60 pieces. A lot of the horn players were from that era, the big band era. So I got to hear the stories. Larry Welk told me great stories. The guy said his father had in the horns were big band guys, and they’d take breaks and Lawrence Welk would go to his dressing room and eat a chicken salad sandwich, they were at the bar down…

was the band boy, running errands for them. So he knew all the stories from these guys. They’d all played with the big bands. They’d put on their suits and do the Lawrence Welk Show. But these guys could swing if they really wanted to, or were allowed to. But I knew a lot of the big band guys. The first time I did the Tonight Show when Johnny Carson was still the host, I mean Severinsen played with Tommy Dorsey, those guys were all, mostly big band alumni. And you heard all the stories, and they were obviously…
Yeah. Did you ever hear those fellas complain or comment about transition from swing to rock & roll?
